📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section

📖 Worked example — a module-info.java, decoded

WORKED EXAMPLE — two modules cooperating
// inventory-api module
module com.shop.api {
    exports com.shop.api.model;      // ONLY this package is visible outside
}

// inventory-app module
module com.shop.app {
    requires com.shop.api;           // I use that module
    requires java.sql;               // and the JDK's SQL module
}
exports controls what leaves a module (unexported packages are invisible even if public!); requires declares dependencies. The compiler enforces both — accidental use of internal packages becomes a compile error instead of tech debt.
⚠️ PUBLIC IS NO LONGER ENOUGH
Inside the module system, a public class in a NON-exported package cannot be touched from outside. “public + exported” is the new visibility rule — the single most-tested module fact.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

The Java module system (Project Jigsaw, Java 9+) addresses long-standing problems: classpath hell, hidden internal APIs, missing ahead-of-time dependency information. It is essential for understanding modern Java distribution and JDK internals — even if you choose not to modularize your application.

Core concepts

1. What a module is. A named, self-describing collection of packages plus a module-info.java file. The module-info declares: which packages it exports, which modules it requires, and what services it provides or uses. It is the unit of distribution above the JAR.

2. module-info.java. module com.example.app { exports com.example.app.api; requires com.fasterxml.jackson.databind; } — exports lists packages other modules can see; requires lists modules this depends on. Compiled into module-info.class at the JAR root.

3. Strong encapsulation. Packages NOT in an exports list are inaccessible to other modules, even with reflection (by default). This is enforced by the JVM, not just compile-time. Internal implementation details stay internal.

4. The JDK is modular. Since Java 9, the JDK itself is split into ~70 modules. java.base — always available. java.sql, java.xml, etc. — must be required. jdk.* modules are JDK-specific and may not be portable.

5. The classpath vs the module path. Pre-Java-9 code uses the classpath — flat, no encapsulation. Modular code uses the module path. They coexist: unnamed modules (classpath) can read named modules; named modules can read each other only via requires.

6. jlink and custom runtimes. jlink creates a minimal Java runtime containing only the modules your app needs. Smaller distribution, faster startup. Especially valuable for containerized deployments — slim Docker images.

7. When to modularize, when not to. Library authors — yes; gives strong encapsulation and clear API. New large applications — consider it. Small applications — usually not worth the cost. Existing apps with messy dependencies — high migration effort. Many production apps still use the classpath.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Reflection that worked on the classpath now fails on modules — requires opens or open module declaration.
  • Forgetting requires for transitively-needed modules — compile errors that aren't always obvious.
  • Using jdk.internal.* APIs — they are not exported by default and can break across releases.
  • Modularizing for the sake of it — many apps add complexity without gaining encapsulation benefit.

Quick recap

Modules are named units above JARs with declared exports and requires. Strong encapsulation hides non-exported packages. The JDK is itself modular. jlink produces minimal runtimes. Modules are most valuable for libraries and large new apps; small apps and legacy systems often stay on the classpath.

Glossary

Module
Self-describing unit with explicit exports and requires.
module-info.java
Source file declaring a module's name, exports, and dependencies.
Strong encapsulation
JVM-enforced hiding of non-exported packages.
Module path
Equivalent of classpath for modular code.
jlink
JDK tool building minimal custom Java runtimes from a set of modules.
"}, "D387/ch5/s4": {"body": "
📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section

📖 Worked example — pattern matching in switch and instanceof

WORKED EXAMPLE — old cast dance vs pattern matching
// old:
if (obj instanceof String) {
    String s = (String) obj;          // test, THEN cast
    use(s.length());
}
// new: test AND bind in one step
if (obj instanceof String s) use(s.length());

// switch patterns + sealed types = exhaustive, no default needed
double area = switch (shape) {
    case Circle c -> Math.PI * c.r() * c.r();
    case Square s -> s.side() * s.side();
};
The pattern variable (s, c) is typed and in scope only where the match succeeded. With a sealed Shape, the compiler verifies every case is covered — add a Triangle later and the switch stops compiling until handled: bugs caught at compile time.
⚠️ ARROW CASES DON’T FALL THROUGH
switch expressions with -> have no fall-through and must be exhaustive (via sealed coverage or default). The old colon-switch rules don’t apply — questions love mixing the two syntaxes.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Pattern matching (Java 16-21) brings Scala-style destructuring to Java. Switch expressions, type patterns, record patterns, sealed-type exhaustiveness — together they replace verbose instanceof-and-cast chains with concise, safer code. They are the most consequential syntax additions to Java in a decade.

Core concepts

1. Switch expressions. switch as an expression, not a statement: var msg = switch (day) { case MON, TUE -> "start"; case FRI -> "end"; default -> "middle"; }; The arrow form is exhaustive (no fall-through), and yield works in block bodies. Cleaner than if-else chains.

2. Pattern matching for instanceof. if (obj instanceof String s) — declares s as the cast variable in the same expression. Eliminates the redundant cast on the next line. Available in conditions, while, ternary.

3. Type patterns in switch. switch (shape) { case Circle c -> Math.PI * c.radius() * c.radius(); case Square s -> s.side() * s.side(); ... }. Each case binds a typed variable. Replaces nested instanceof chains with one expressive switch.

4. Record patterns (Java 21). Destructure records inside patterns: case Point(int x, int y) -> x + y. Combine with switch type patterns: case Circle(Point center, double r) -> ... Reads the structure directly; no manual accessor calls.

5. Sealed types + switch = exhaustive. If the matched type is sealed, the compiler verifies that all permitted subtypes are covered. Missing a case is a compile error. No 'default' needed; the compiler proves you handled everything.

6. When-clauses for guards (Java 21). case Point p when p.x() > 0 -> "positive"; — additional condition narrowing the match. Guards make pattern matching expressive enough to replace many if-else trees.

7. The bigger picture. Records (data) + sealed types (closed hierarchy) + pattern matching (destructure and switch) = modern Java's answer to functional algebraic data types. The trio is what Scala, Kotlin, OCaml, F#, and Rust have had for years; Java caught up.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Mixing arrow-form and colon-form switches — pick one per switch.
  • Using non-sealed types in pattern switches and assuming completeness — compiler can't verify, you need a default.
  • Forgetting that switch on null is allowed (Java 21+) only with a null case — otherwise NPE.
  • Over-using guards to express logic that should be a method — guards work best for simple narrowing.

Quick recap

Switch expressions, instanceof patterns, switch type patterns, record patterns, when-guards, and sealed-type exhaustiveness combine into modern Java pattern matching. They replace instanceof-and-cast chains with concise, type-safe, exhaustively-checked code.

Glossary

Switch expression
switch as a value-producing expression with arrow cases and yield.
Type pattern
obj instanceof Type t — binds the cast variable in the same expression.
Record pattern
Destructure record components inline: case Point(int x, int y).
Sealed exhaustiveness
Compiler checks all permitted subtypes are handled in a switch.
When-clause
Guard condition on a pattern case for additional matching logic.
"}, "D387/ch6/s1": {"body": "
📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section

📖 Worked example — Singleton & Builder (creational patterns)

WORKED EXAMPLE — both patterns, minimal and correct
// SINGLETON — exactly one instance, globally reachable
public class Config {
    private static final Config INSTANCE = new Config();
    private Config() { }                      // nobody else constructs
    public static Config get() { return INSTANCE; }
}

// BUILDER — readable construction of many-argument objects
Pizza p = new Pizza.Builder()
        .size("L").cheese(true).mushrooms(true)
        .build();
Singleton = private constructor + one static instance. Builder = chainable setters ending in build(), replacing a 7-argument constructor nobody can read. Factory Method rounds out the trio: a method decides WHICH subclass to construct and returns the supertype.
⚠️ RECOGNIZE BY SYMPTOM
“Exactly one instance” → Singleton. “Telescoping constructors / many optional parameters” → Builder. “Creation logic varies by type, callers shouldn’t know the class” → Factory. Exams describe the symptom, never the name.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Creational patterns control how objects are made. Singleton, Factory, Builder, Prototype — used right, they keep object construction flexible and decoupled. Used reflexively, they create unnecessary indirection. Knowing each pattern's actual problem prevents you from applying it where simpler code would do.

Core concepts

1. Singleton — one instance ever. Ensures a class has exactly one instance and provides global access. The Java idiomatic implementation: enum Singleton { INSTANCE; ... } — thread-safe, serialization-safe, reflection-safe. Other implementations (double-checked locking, lazy holder) work but have subtle issues.

2. When NOT to Singleton. Almost always. Singletons are global state in disguise. They make code hard to test (no easy injection of mocks), couple unrelated modules, and proliferate fast. Prefer dependency injection: pass the single instance into constructors.

3. Factory Method. A method that returns a new object, hiding the choice of concrete type. List.of, Optional.of, Files.newBufferedReader — all factory methods. Cleaner than exposing constructors when the type might evolve.

4. Abstract Factory. A family of factory methods producing related objects. Less common in modern Java, where dependency injection frameworks usually fill the same role. Still valuable for cross-platform UIs and test/production swaps.

5. Builder. For constructing complex objects with many optional parameters. Fluent API: new Pizza.Builder().crust(THIN).cheese(true).topping(PEPPERONI).build(). Replaces telescoping constructors. Lombok's @Builder generates this automatically; records may eliminate the need for many simple builders.

6. Prototype. Clone an existing object as the basis for a new one. Useful when construction is expensive or configuration is hierarchical. Implement Cloneable and override clone — though deep-copy semantics need care, and many teams use copy constructors or libraries instead.

7. When patterns help vs hurt. Use Singleton only via DI (or for true OS-level resources). Use Factory when concrete types vary or evolve. Use Builder when constructors have many optional parameters. Use Prototype only for genuine clone use cases. Don't apply patterns by default — apply them when the problem actually appears.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Singleton-everywhere — global state in disguise, hostile to testing.
  • Factories hiding what you actually wanted (a constructor) — adds layers without adding clarity.
  • Builders for classes with three fields — Lombok @Builder or a record is enough.
  • Cloning with shallow-copy when deep-copy was needed — bugs surface as 'why is this list shared?'

Quick recap

Singleton — rarely; via DI when at all. Factory — when types may vary. Builder — for many optional parameters. Prototype — for genuine cloning. Each pattern solves a real problem; reflexively applying patterns is its own anti-pattern.

Glossary

Singleton
Pattern ensuring exactly one instance of a class.
Factory Method
Method that returns objects, hiding concrete type choice.
Abstract Factory
Family of factories producing related objects.
Builder
Pattern for stepwise construction of complex objects.
Prototype
Pattern of cloning an existing instance to produce new ones.
"}, "D387/ch6/s2": {"body": "

📖 Worked example — Adapter & Decorator (structural patterns)

WORKED EXAMPLE — both patterns in 12 lines
// ADAPTER — make an old interface fit a new one
class LegacyPrinter { void printOld(String s) { ... } }
class PrinterAdapter implements ModernPrinter {
    private LegacyPrinter legacy = new LegacyPrinter();
    public void print(String s) { legacy.printOld(s); }   // translate the call
}

// DECORATOR — add behavior by WRAPPING, not subclassing
InputStream in = new BufferedInputStream(
                   new FileInputStream("data.txt"));   // buffering wraps file IO
Adapter translates between incompatible interfaces (a plug converter). Decorator wraps an object with the SAME interface and adds a layer — Java’s I/O streams are the canonical stack of decorators. Facade (one simple front door over a messy subsystem) completes the structural trio.
⚠️ ADAPTER CHANGES THE INTERFACE, DECORATOR KEEPS IT
That one sentence separates them on every quiz. Wrapping + same interface + added behavior = decorator; wrapping + translated interface = adapter.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Structural patterns control how classes and objects compose into larger structures. Adapter, Decorator, Facade, Proxy, Composite — they are the toolkit for fitting incompatible APIs together, layering behavior, simplifying complex subsystems. The Java standard library uses every one heavily.

Core concepts

1. Adapter — make incompatible interfaces talk. Wraps one interface to look like another. java.io.InputStreamReader adapts a byte InputStream to a char Reader. Whenever you need to bridge two libraries that disagree on interface shape, you need an Adapter.

2. Decorator — layer behavior dynamically. Wraps an object to add behavior without subclassing. new BufferedReader(new FileReader(file)) — FileReader provides reading; BufferedReader adds buffering. Each layer implements the same interface, allowing arbitrary composition.

3. Facade — simplified entry to a complex subsystem. Hides internal complexity behind a small, task-focused API. javax.persistence.EntityManager is a facade over the JPA implementation's many internal classes. Lets callers use the system without knowing its parts.

4. Proxy — stand in for the real object. Same interface as the real subject; controls access. Spring's @Transactional generates proxies that wrap method calls in transaction lifecycle. Lazy loading proxies, security proxies, remote proxies — same pattern, different motivation.

5. Composite — treat groups uniformly with single objects. Both leaves and containers implement the same interface. java.io.File treats files and directories as the same kind of thing. UI component trees use this everywhere. Recursion becomes natural.

6. Bridge — separate abstraction from implementation. Splits a class that varies in two dimensions into two hierarchies. java.awt.Toolkit (the abstraction) and platform-specific peers (the implementation). Less common in modern code; dependency injection often fills the role.

7. Flyweight — share fine-grained objects. Reuses immutable instances when many duplicates would be created. Integer.valueOf caches small integers. String interning. Useful when a system creates millions of small immutable objects.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Confusing Adapter and Decorator — Adapter changes interface; Decorator preserves interface and adds behavior.
  • Facade hiding too much — callers can't reach what they actually need; design for the 80% case.
  • Decorator chains so deep that debugging requires unwinding 10 layers.
  • Composite without a unified interface — leaves and containers branch in client code, defeating the pattern.

Quick recap

Adapter for interface translation. Decorator for layered behavior. Facade for simplified entry. Proxy for controlled access. Composite for uniform tree-like structures. Bridge for two-dimensional variation. Flyweight for shared immutable instances. Each names a real recurring problem.

Glossary

Adapter
Wraps an object to expose a different interface.
Decorator
Wraps an object to add behavior while preserving the same interface.
Facade
Simplified entry point hiding a complex subsystem.
Proxy
Stand-in for an object that controls access (lazy load, security, remote).
Composite
Tree structure where leaves and branches implement the same interface.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Adapter and Decorator side by side, executed
interface Notifier { String send(String msg); }                      // what our code expects

class LegacySmsGateway {                                             // cannot be changed
  String transmit(String body, int priority) { return "SMS[p" + priority + "]:" + body; }
}

// ADAPTER — translates one interface into another
class SmsAdapter implements Notifier {
  private final LegacySmsGateway legacy = new LegacySmsGateway();
  public String send(String msg) { return legacy.transmit(msg, 1); }
}

// DECORATOR — same interface in, same interface out, one extra layer
abstract class NotifierDecorator implements Notifier {
  protected final Notifier inner;
  NotifierDecorator(Notifier inner) { this.inner = inner; }
}
class Timestamped extends NotifierDecorator {
  Timestamped(Notifier n) { super(n); }
  public String send(String m) { return inner.send("[mon 09:00] " + m); }
}
class Uppercase extends NotifierDecorator {
  Uppercase(Notifier n) { super(n); }
  public String send(String m) { return inner.send(m.toUpperCase()); }
}

public class Demo {
  public static void main(String[] a) {
    Notifier base = new SmsAdapter();
    System.out.println("adapter only        : " + base.send("deploy ok"));
    System.out.println("+ Timestamped       : " + new Timestamped(base).send("deploy ok"));
    System.out.println("+ Uppercase(Timest.): " + new Uppercase(new Timestamped(base)).send("deploy ok"));
    System.out.println("+ Timest.(Uppercase): " + new Timestamped(new Uppercase(base)).send("deploy ok"));
  }
}

Output (this program was compiled and run on JDK 21):

adapter only        : SMS[p1]:deploy ok
+ Timestamped       : SMS[p1]:[mon 09:00] deploy ok
+ Uppercase(Timest.): SMS[p1]:[mon 09:00] DEPLOY OK
+ Timest.(Uppercase): SMS[p1]:[MON 09:00] DEPLOY OK

Step 1 — the adapter. The client only knows send(String). LegacySmsGateway only offers transmit(String, int). SmsAdapter implements the expected interface and translates the call, supplying the priority the client never knew about. The interface CHANGED across the wrapper.

Step 2 — one decorator. Timestamped also wraps a Notifier, but it implements Notifier itself. The interface is IDENTICAL on both sides, so the client cannot tell a decorated notifier from a plain one.

Step 3 — stacking. Because every layer has the same type, they compose freely: new Uppercase(new Timestamped(base)) is still just a Notifier. That is why java.io lets you write new DataInputStream(new BufferedInputStream(new FileInputStream(f))).

Step 4 — order is visible in the output. Compare the last two lines. Uppercase(Timestamped(base)) uppercases first and then prepends the stamp, giving [mon 09:00] DEPLOY OK. Timestamped(Uppercase(base)) prepends first, so the stamp itself gets uppercased: [MON 09:00] DEPLOY OK. Same layers, different order, different result.

The trap: both patterns are "a class that holds another object", so students match them by shape. Match them by the interface instead: translated interface = Adapter, preserved interface = Decorator. A Facade is the third relative — it fronts a whole subsystem with a new, simpler interface rather than wrapping one object.

Figure — Same wrapping shape, opposite intent: the adapter translates one interface into another, the decorator keeps the interface and adds a layer.

📖 Worked example — Observer & Strategy (behavioral patterns)

WORKED EXAMPLE — both patterns, minimal
// OBSERVER — subscribers notified on change
class Stock {
    private List<Runnable> observers = new ArrayList<>();
    void subscribe(Runnable r) { observers.add(r); }
    void priceChanged() { observers.forEach(Runnable::run); }
}
stock.subscribe(() -> System.out.println("alert!"));

// STRATEGY — swap the algorithm at runtime
list.sort((a, b) -> a.length() - b.length());   // strategy #1: by length
list.sort(String::compareTo);                    // strategy #2: alphabetical
Observer = one-to-many notification (event listeners, pub/sub). Strategy = interchangeable algorithms behind one interface — every Comparator you pass to sort IS a strategy. Command (actions as objects, undo queues) rounds out the trio.
⚠️ SPOT THEM IN THE WILD
“When X changes, notify all Y” → Observer. “Choose the algorithm at runtime” → Strategy. “Queue/undo user actions” → Command. The behavioral patterns are recognized by their VERBS.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Behavioral patterns control how objects communicate and divide responsibility. Strategy, Observer, Command, Iterator, State, Template Method, Chain of Responsibility — they describe how to organize behavior cleanly. Java standard library and Spring lean on them everywhere; recognizing them helps you read framework code.

Core concepts

1. Strategy — interchangeable algorithms. Encapsulates an algorithm behind an interface and makes it interchangeable at runtime. Comparator implementations are strategies for sorting. Lambda support makes Strategy almost free in modern Java — just pass a lambda.

2. Observer — publish-subscribe. Defines one-to-many dependency: when subject changes, observers are notified. java.beans.PropertyChangeListener, JavaFX observables, reactive streams (Flow.Subscriber) — all observers under different names. The basis of event-driven UI.

3. Command — encapsulate a request as an object. A request becomes an object: parameters, target, executable. Enables queuing, logging, undo, transaction batching. Runnable is essentially Command. Action classes in Swing, command handlers in CQRS — same pattern.

4. Iterator — sequential access to elements. Hides collection internals while exposing element-by-element traversal. java.util.Iterator. Java's enhanced for loop uses Iterable behind the scenes. Streams generalize iterators with declarative pipelines.

5. State — vary behavior with internal state. Object's behavior changes as its state changes. A vending machine class delegates handleCoin to a state object whose implementation differs by current state (idle, has-coins, dispensing). Replaces giant switch statements over status enums.

6. Template Method — fixed skeleton, customizable steps. Abstract method calls fill in the variations. AbstractList.iterator uses template method calling abstract get and size. Frameworks (Spring, JUnit) use it heavily.

7. Chain of Responsibility — pass the request along. A chain of handlers, each can handle the request or pass it on. Servlet filters, exception handlers, middleware in web frameworks — all chains. Decouples sender from receiver and lets handlers be added or removed dynamically.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Strategy pattern with anonymous classes pre-Java-8 was ugly; with lambdas it's nearly invisible — don't over-engineer.
  • Observer with too many observers — performance and ordering issues; consider a message bus.
  • Command pattern for every method call — complexity not justified by the lack of queuing/undo needs.
  • State pattern for two-state systems — boolean flags are fine; state is for genuinely multi-state behavior.

Quick recap

Strategy — swap algorithms. Observer — notify many. Command — request as object. Iterator — sequential access. State — vary by internal state. Template Method — fixed skeleton, customizable steps. Chain of Responsibility — pass request along handlers. Each names a real problem in real frameworks.

Glossary

Strategy
Pattern encapsulating interchangeable algorithms behind an interface.
Observer
Pattern for subjects to notify many observers of state changes.
Command
Pattern wrapping a request as an object for queuing, logging, undo.
State
Pattern delegating behavior to a state object whose implementation varies.
Chain of Responsibility
Pattern of handlers each deciding to handle a request or pass it along.
📊 FIGURE — Memento: undo without breaking encapsulation
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — A text editor with undo
Editor ed = new Editor();
java.util.Deque<Editor.Memento> history = new java.util.ArrayDeque<>();

ed.type("Hello");
history.push(ed.save());
ed.type(", world");
history.push(ed.save());
ed.type("!!!");

System.out.println("now:      " + ed.getText());
ed.restore(history.pop());
System.out.println("undo 1:   " + ed.getText());
ed.restore(history.pop());
System.out.println("undo 2:   " + ed.getText());
now: Hello, world!!! undo 1: Hello, world undo 2: Hello
actual output, captured from the JVM
  1. The caretaker here is the Deque: it stores mementos and hands them back, but the memento's field is private so it can never inspect or alter the state.
  2. Only the Originator can create a memento and only the Originator can read one back — that is what "without violating encapsulation" means.
  3. Push a snapshot before each change and undo becomes a pop.
🎯 EXAM TIP
Memento is the snapshot/undo pattern. If a question describes capturing an object's state so it can be rolled back later, without exposing that object's internals to whoever stores it, the answer is Memento — not Observer (notification) and not Command (which can also do undo, but by storing the operation rather than the state).

📖 Worked example — localizing an app with ResourceBundle

WORKED EXAMPLE — English/French in four steps
# messages_en.properties        # messages_fr.properties
greeting=Welcome!               greeting=Bienvenue!

Locale fr = Locale.forLanguageTag("fr");
ResourceBundle msgs = ResourceBundle.getBundle("messages", fr);
System.out.println(msgs.getString("greeting"));   // Bienvenue!

// numbers & currency localize too:
NumberFormat.getCurrencyInstance(Locale.FRANCE).format(9.99); // 9,99 €
DateTimeFormatter.ofLocalizedDate(FormatStyle.LONG)
                 .withLocale(fr).format(LocalDate.now());
One properties file per language, keys shared; the bundle picks the file matching the Locale (falling back to the default when a translation is missing). Currency, dates, and number separators all come from the SAME Locale object — never hard-code formats.
⚠️ FILE NAMING IS THE MECHANISM
messages_fr.properties matches Locale “fr” by NAME. Typo the suffix and you silently get English (fallback), not an error — the sneaky localization bug the PA makes you chase.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Software that ships only to English-speaking users in one timezone is rare. Internationalization (i18n) is the discipline of making software adapt to locale, language, currency, date format, plurals, and text direction. Done right at the start, it costs little; retrofit is painful.

Core concepts

1. Locale — the user's cultural context. java.util.Locale represents a language plus optionally country and variant: Locale.US, Locale.JAPAN, new Locale("es", "MX"). Determines how dates, numbers, and currency format. Often comes from the user's browser or OS settings.

2. Resource bundles for translatable strings. ResourceBundle.getBundle("messages", locale) loads messages_en.properties, messages_ja.properties, etc. Strings live in property files keyed by name. Code references the key, not the literal string. The foundation of every multilingual Java app.

3. Number, currency, date formatting. NumberFormat.getInstance(locale), NumberFormat.getCurrencyInstance(locale), DateTimeFormatter.ofLocalizedDate(FormatStyle.MEDIUM).withLocale(locale). Each respects locale conventions: "1,234.56" vs "1.234,56", "$" vs "€" vs "¥", date order, calendar systems.

4. MessageFormat for parameterized messages. Some translations require word order changes. MessageFormat.format("You have {0} new messages from {1}", count, sender). Translators reorder placeholders without code changes. Strings with concatenated fragments are an i18n anti-pattern.

5. Pluralization is hard. English: 1 message, 2 messages. Russian: 1 сообщение, 2 сообщения, 5 сообщений. ChoiceFormat or ICU's MessageFormat handle plural variants. Don't naively concatenate "s" — it works for English and breaks for almost everyone else.

6. Text direction and RTL. Arabic, Hebrew, Persian read right-to-left. UI layout must mirror; some characters change shape based on neighbors. Java handles bidirectional text via java.text.Bidi. Beyond text: layouts (CSS, JavaFX) need RTL-aware mirroring.

7. Character encoding — assume UTF-8 always. Modern Java uses UTF-8 by default for source files (Java 18+) and most I/O. For older code or external interfaces, always specify Charset explicitly: Files.readString(path, StandardCharsets.UTF_8). Never trust platform default.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Concatenating translatable strings: "Hello " + name + ", you have " + count + " messages" — translators can't reorder.
  • Hardcoding date or number formats — breaks for any non-default locale.
  • Using new String(bytes) without specifying charset — platform default, unpredictable.
  • Naive pluralization ("s" suffix) — works for English; breaks for everything else.

Quick recap

Locale captures cultural context. Resource bundles externalize translatable strings. Format classes respect locale conventions for numbers, currency, dates. MessageFormat handles word order; ChoiceFormat handles plurals. Always specify UTF-8 explicitly when working with byte streams. i18n is design, not retrofit.

Glossary

Locale
User's language, country, variant for cultural formatting.
ResourceBundle
Externalized translatable strings keyed by name.
MessageFormat
Parameterized message formatter supporting reordering for translation.
DateTimeFormatter
Locale-aware date and time formatter (java.time).
UTF-8
Universal character encoding; modern Java default and the right choice for I/O.

📖 Worked example — files with NIO.2’s Path API

WORKED EXAMPLE — the modern file toolkit
Path p = Path.of("data", "report.txt");     // data/report.txt
Files.writeString(p, "hello");               // write
String text = Files.readString(p);           // read it back
List<String> lines = Files.readAllLines(p);
Files.exists(p);          // true
Files.copy(p, Path.of("data", "backup.txt"));

try (Stream<String> s = Files.lines(p)) {    // stream a big file lazily
    long n = s.filter(l -> l.contains("error")).count();
}
Path models the location; Files does the operations. Files.lines plugs straight into the Streams API — grep-like processing in two lines, with try-with-resources closing the file.
⚠️ Path REPLACES File
The legacy java.io.File returns booleans on failure (silently); NIO.2 throws IOException with real diagnostics, handles links/permissions, and streams directories. “Which API should new code use?” → Path/Files, with checked-exception handling.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

java.io.File predates a decade of file-system features and has a clumsy API. java.nio.file (NIO.2, since Java 7) is the modern replacement: Path objects, Files utility, file system events, asynchronous I/O. Modern Java code uses NIO.2; legacy code uses File. Knowing both, but writing new code with NIO.2, is the standard.

Core concepts

1. Path is the modern File. Paths.get("/tmp/data.txt") or Path.of("/tmp/data.txt") — represents a path without verifying existence. Methods: getFileName, getParent, resolve, relativize. Far cleaner API than File.

2. Files — the utility class. Files.readString(path), Files.writeString(path, content), Files.copy, Files.move, Files.delete, Files.exists, Files.size. Most operations you used to do with File or FileInputStream are now one Files.* call.

3. Reading and writing files. Files.readAllLines(path) — small files into a list. Files.lines(path) — stream of lines (use try-with-resources). Files.readString and writeString — entire file as String. Files.newBufferedReader / Writer for streaming.

4. Walking directory trees. Files.walk(path) — Stream of all entries. Files.list(path) — direct children only. Files.find(path, depth, predicate) — filtered walk. Combined with streams, directory traversal becomes one expressive line.

5. WatchService — file system events. Path.register(watchService, ENTRY_CREATE, ENTRY_MODIFY, ENTRY_DELETE) lets you receive events when files change. Useful for hot-reload, log monitoring, configuration changes. Polls under the hood on most platforms but exposes a uniform API.

6. File attributes. Files.readAttributes(path, BasicFileAttributes.class) — size, creation time, modification time, isDirectory. PosixFileAttributes for Unix permissions. Faster than separate exists/isDirectory/lastModified calls because attributes come from one stat() call.

7. Async file I/O — AsynchronousFileChannel. Non-blocking file reads and writes returning Future or invoking CompletionHandler. Useful for very high-throughput servers. Most apps don't need it; standard Files.* is sufficient.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Using java.io.File in new code — legacy API; harder to test, fewer features.
  • Files.lines without try-with-resources — file handle leak.
  • Repeated existence checks before each operation — race condition; just attempt and handle the exception.
  • Hard-coded path separators — use Path.resolve and let the OS pick / or \.

Quick recap

Path replaces File for representing locations. Files provides every operation as a static method. Files.walk and Files.lines pair beautifully with streams. WatchService observes file system changes. Read attributes in one call rather than several. Async I/O exists for niche high-throughput cases.

Glossary

Path
NIO.2 representation of a file system path; replaces File.
Files
Utility class with static methods for nearly every file operation.
WatchService
Observer for file system change events.
BasicFileAttributes
Object holding size, timestamps, and type from one stat call.
AsynchronousFileChannel
Non-blocking file channel returning Future or invoking CompletionHandler.

📖 Worked example — object ↔ JSON round trip

WORKED EXAMPLE — serialize out, parse back
public record Customer(String name, int points) { }

ObjectMapper mapper = new ObjectMapper();          // Jackson
String json = mapper.writeValueAsString(new Customer("Amara", 120));
// {"name":"Amara","points":120}

Customer back = mapper.readValue(json, Customer.class);
back.points();      // 120 — full round trip
Serialization = object → transportable text; deserialization = text → object. Field names become JSON keys automatically (customizable with @JsonProperty). This is exactly what @RestController does under the hood on every request/response.
⚠️ JSON vs JAVA SERIALIZATION
Java’s built-in Serializable produces a binary, Java-only format with known security issues; JSON is text, language-neutral, and web-standard. For APIs the answer is always JSON — Serializable appears on exams mostly as the thing NOT to choose.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Objects often need to leave the JVM — to disk, over a network, into a database. Serialization formats are how. Java's built-in Serializable has known security issues; Jackson and Gson dominate JSON; Protocol Buffers and Avro dominate binary. Knowing each format's tradeoffs picks the right tool per use case.

Core concepts

1. Java Serializable — built-in but problematic. implements Serializable and the JVM can write/read object graphs. Trivially easy. But: insecure (deserialization attacks), version-fragile, opaque, slow. Modern code rarely uses it for anything beyond legacy interop.

2. JSON with Jackson. ObjectMapper.writeValueAsString(obj), readValue(json, Class). Annotations for naming, ignoring, polymorphism (@JsonProperty, @JsonIgnore, @JsonTypeInfo). The de facto Java JSON library. Spring Boot includes it by default.

3. JSON with Gson. Google's alternative. new Gson().toJson(obj) and fromJson(json, Class). Simpler API, fewer features. Either works; Jackson dominates in Spring ecosystems, Gson in some Android codebases.

4. Polymorphic JSON — handle subtypes. Serializing a sealed Shape hierarchy back as Circle or Square requires type info. @JsonTypeInfo with NAME and @JsonSubTypes annotations make it work. Otherwise Jackson serializes Shape but can't distinguish on deserialization.

5. Records and JSON (Java 16+). Records are first-class JSON citizens — Jackson handles them with the right annotations or a Jackson module. Combined with sealed types, JSON for sum types is natural in modern Java.

6. Binary formats — Protocol Buffers, Avro, MessagePack. When JSON's verbosity costs too much (size, parse time): Protobuf (Google) and Avro (Apache) define schemas, generate code, produce compact binary. Schema evolution is supported. Dominant in microservices and big-data pipelines.

7. Choosing a format. JSON — human-readable, web-standard, Jackson-supported. Java Serializable — avoid except for compatibility. Protobuf/Avro — high-throughput services, schema-evolution needs. CBOR/MessagePack — JSON-like but binary. Match format to constraints (size, speed, schema management).

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Implementing Serializable on classes accepting untrusted input — deserialization gadget chain attacks are real.
  • Forgetting @JsonProperty when JSON keys differ from field names — silent data loss.
  • Serializing entities directly to API consumers — leaks internal fields and creates coupling. Use DTOs.
  • Choosing JSON for high-throughput internal services where Protobuf would save 80% of bandwidth.

Quick recap

Java Serializable is legacy; modern serialization is JSON via Jackson or Gson, with Protobuf/Avro for binary needs. Annotations control naming, polymorphism, ignored fields. Records integrate cleanly. Always use DTOs for external boundaries; never expose internal entities. Pick format by constraints, not familiarity.

Glossary

Serializable
Java's built-in serialization; legacy, security concerns, rarely used in new code.
Jackson
De facto Java JSON library; ObjectMapper at its core.
@JsonProperty
Annotation overriding the JSON key name for a field.
Polymorphic JSON
JSON serialization handling subtype hierarchies via type information.
Protocol Buffers (Protobuf)
Compact binary serialization with schema-driven code generation.

📖 Worked example — mapping a code-PA requirement to the build

WORKED EXAMPLE — “display the message in two languages” style tasks
Code PAs hand you a starter project and a numbered requirement list. The winning loop, per requirement:

1. Find the touchpoint — which class/file the requirement lives in (search the starter for related names).
2. Implement with the course tool — a localization requirement wants ResourceBundle/Locale (ch7); a concurrency requirement wants threads/ExecutorService done SAFELY (ch4) — the graders check you used the taught mechanism, not a workaround.
3. Run and verify visibly — the app must SHOW the behavior (both languages printed, both threads logging).
4. Commit with a message naming the requirement (“Add French welcome via ResourceBundle”) — the history maps commits to requirements one-to-one.

Requirements are independent slices: finish one completely (code + run + commit) before opening the next.

The deliverable

D387 Advanced Java is a Performance Assessment (PA): there is no objective test. You take an existing Spring Boot application — most students reuse the project they built in D288 Back-End Programming — and add a set of advanced Java capabilities. You then push the enhanced code to a GitLab repository and submit a written narrative (and frequently a Panopto screen-recording) that walks the evaluator through what you changed and where.

The four enhancements

The task centers on four competencies. Exact wording and lettering change over time, so confirm your current task instructions, but the substance is stable:

  • Multithreading / concurrency — run work concurrently using ExecutorService with Callable/Future, a thread pool, or parallel streams. It must genuinely execute in parallel, not just look threaded.
  • Functional programming — replace imperative loops with lambdas and the Streams API (map, filter, collect, reduce).
  • Internationalization (i18n) — externalize UI text into ResourceBundle .properties files for at least two locales (English plus one other) and let the app switch locale.
  • Containerization — write a Dockerfile, build an image, and run the app inside a container. Many tasks also want a GitLab CI pipeline and/or a written cloud-deployment plan.

How it's submitted

You provide the GitLab repo URL (make sure the evaluator has access), a document that explicitly maps each rubric feature to the file and line/class where you implemented it, and typically a Panopto link demonstrating the running, containerized app. The single most common cause of a return is a submission that adds the feature but never explains where it lives.

Anchor to your current official task instructions and rubric — WGU revises exact aspect wording periodically.

📖 Worked example — reading a code-PA rubric aspect

WORKED EXAMPLE — “the submission implements the required threading”
What the evaluator does: opens your repo, finds the relevant class, checks the mechanism (real threads/pool, shared state handled safely), runs the app, and looks for the visible output the requirement names.

Competent: the taught mechanism, working, visible at runtime.
Returned: code that compiles but never runs the second thread; sleeps faking concurrency; output not demonstrable; or the mechanism replaced with something off-syllabus.

Per aspect, ask: can a stranger clone, run, and SEE this requirement working in under a minute? If yes with screenshots to match, the aspect passes.

Passing each competency

Every rubric aspect is scored pass/fail against evidence in your repo. Give the evaluator proof — a real concurrent execution, a real stream pipeline, real .properties files, a real image that builds and runs — and a narrative that points to it.

CompetencyWhat evaluators look forHow to nail it
Concurrency / multithreadingWork that actually runs on multiple threads simultaneously, not sequential code labeled 'threaded'.Use an ExecutorService thread pool submitting Callable tasks and collecting Future results, or a well-justified parallelStream(). Log thread names to prove concurrency.
Functional programming & streamsImperative loops replaced by lambdas and the Streams API.Convert a for-loop into a stream().filter().map().collect() pipeline; use method references and functional interfaces where natural.
Localization / i18nUI strings pulled from ResourceBundle files for 2+ locales, switchable at runtime.Create messages_en.properties and e.g. messages_es.properties; load via ResourceBundle.getBundle or Spring MessageSource and drive display off the selected Locale. Code quality & documentationReadable code, comments, and a narrative locating each feature.Comment each enhanced block and write a doc that names the file/class/line for every rubric feature.

Common trap

Evaluators verify claims against the code. If your write-up says 'multithreading in the report service' but the method runs sequentially, it fails. Make each claim independently checkable.

📖 Worked example — the pre-submit sweep for a code PA

WORKED EXAMPLE — a returned submission, diagnosed
Case: “localization not evident” — the student added the French properties file but never switched the Locale, so the app only ever printed English. Compiles ≠ demonstrates.

The sweep before submitting:
1. Fresh clone in a NEW folder; build and run from scratch (catches files that never got committed).
2. Walk the requirement list top to bottom, watching each behavior actually happen; screenshot each.
3. Commit history: multiple commits with messages that map to requirements.
4. No leftover TODOs, debug prints, or commented-out chunks in graded files.
5. Submission includes exactly what the task asks (repo link, screenshots, notes) — verified against the task page, not memory.

Pre-submission checklist

  1. Concurrency really runs in parallel. Prove it: log thread names, or show tasks completing out of order. A single-threaded method labeled 'multithreaded' is the top return reason.
  2. Streams replace real loops. Point to a before/after where a for-loop became a stream pipeline with lambdas.
  3. i18n is ResourceBundle-driven. At least two locale files (e.g. _en and one other), loaded via ResourceBundle/MessageSource, with locale switching demonstrated. No hard-coded translations.
  4. Dockerfile builds AND runs. Run docker build -t app . then docker run -p 8080:8080 app on a clean machine before submitting. A Dockerfile that doesn't build is an automatic return.
  5. Feature-location narrative. Write a document naming the file, class, and method for each rubric feature. 'Missing explanation of WHERE each feature was added' is a frequent return.
  6. GitLab access & history. Confirm the evaluator can open the repo, commits are present, and any required GitLab CI pipeline file (.gitlab-ci.yml) is included if the task asks for it.
  7. Panopto demo (if required) shows the app running, ideally from the container, and the locale switch working.

Why PAs get returned

🧠 The Aistote Method (J-Method)

THE IDEA
The Aistote app is built on two of the most evidence-backed study techniques — active recall and spaced repetition — run in short, intense 25-minute blocks (its "J-Method"). Instead of slowly re-reading, you spend the time testing yourself and re-testing what you miss. This app already has every tool the method needs.
THE 3-STEP LOOP
StepWhat you doWhere in this app
1. ConvertTurn the material into questions instead of re-reading it.Open a section, skim the lesson once, then jump to its Quiz.
2. RecallAnswer from memory first — no peeking — then check.Take the section Quiz, or a PA / OA simulation; rate your confidence.
3. Space itRe-test only what you missed, on a growing schedule.Every miss becomes a Flashcard; review them on the app's spaced-repetition schedule.
A 25-MINUTE J-METHOD SESSION
TimeDo this
0–3 minSkim the lesson's key terms and the big idea — don't memorize yet, just get the lay of the land.
3–18 minTake the section quiz (or a 15-question drill). Try to recall the answer first, reveal it after.
18–23 minRedo only the questions you got wrong.
23–25 minSend the stubborn ones to Flashcards and note tomorrow's quick review.
Start the block with the ⚡ Focus timer (25 min) on any lesson — that is your J-Method session.
⚠️ THE ONE RULE
Always try to answer from memory before you look. The effort of retrieving is what actually builds the memory — re-reading feels productive but barely moves it.
WHY IT WORKS
Active recall (testing yourself) forces your brain to reconstruct the answer, which strengthens it far more than recognition. Spaced repetition reviews each fact just as you're about to forget it, moving it into long-term memory with the fewest reps. The 25-minute block simply makes you actually do both, every day.
DAILY RHYTHM
Two or three 25-minute J-Method blocks a day (new material in one, missed-question review in the next) beats a single long cram session — and it's how the Aistote method delivers "learn it in 25 minutes" instead of hours.

📋 Functional Programming in Java

Condensed from your lessons — the rules, traps and topics of this chapter in one place.

Lambda Expressions

⚠ ONE ABSTRACT METHOD REQUIRED Lambdas only work where the target type is a functional interface (exactly one abstract method). Two abstract methods → no lambda possible — the compiler error, not a style choice.

Functional Interfaces

⚠ MATCH THE SHAPE, NOT THE NAME Exam questions describe a lambda and ask its interface: look at what goes IN and what comes OUT. () → value is Supplier; value → boolean is Predicate; value → value is Function; value →…

Method and Constructor References

⚠ String::toUpperCase HAS A HIDDEN PARAMETER ClassName::instanceMethod means call it ON the first lambda parameter — s.toUpperCase(). That s different from object::method, where the receiver is fixed. Distinguishing the four reference kinds — static, instance-on-first-parameter, instance-on-a-fixed-object, constructor — is a guaranteed exam item.

"}, "D387/cheat/c2": {"body": "

📋 The Streams API

Condensed from your lessons — the rules, traps and topics of this chapter in one place.

Stream Basics and Pipelines

Core concepts — 1. A stream is not a collection. It is a sequence of elements with a pipeline of operations attached. Streams don't store data; they describe computation. list.stream()…

Quick recap — A stream pipeline has a source, intermediate ops, and one terminal. Operations are lazy; terminals trigger. Streams are single-use. Order operations to filter early. Use…

Glossary

Intermediate Operations

⚠ NO TERMINAL, NO WORK A chain ending at .map(...) with no collect/forEach/count literally never executes — laziness is a graded fact. And streams are single-use: consuming one twice throws IllegalStateException.

Terminal Operations and Collectors

⚠ collect vs reduce Both terminate, but collect builds CONTAINERS (lists, maps, joined strings) and reduce folds to a SINGLE value. Which produces a Map of employees by department? → collect(groupingBy(...)), every…

Parallel Streams

⚠ PARALLEL ISN T FREE Splitting/merging has overhead: small lists or cheap operations often run SLOWER in parallel. And ordering costs extra (forEachOrdered). Default to sequential; measure before parallelizing — that's the exam-safe answer whenever a question asks when parallel streams help.

"}, "D387/cheat/c3": {"body": "

📋 Generics and Collections

Condensed from your lessons — the rules, traps and topics of this chapter in one place.

Generic Classes and Methods

⚠ ERASURE — GENERICS VANISH AT RUNTIME At runtime Box<String> and Box<Integer> are the same class (type erasure): no T.class, no new T(), and instanceof Box<String> won t compile. Generics are a COMPILE-TIME contract.

Bounded Type Parameters and Wildcards

⚠ CAN T ADD TO ? extends Into a List<? extends Number> you may add NOTHING (except null) — it might really be a List<Integer> and you might be holding a Double. Read-only-ness of extends is the most-tested consequence.

Collections Framework Deep Dive

⚠ HASH COLLECTIONS NEED THE CONTRACT HashSet/HashMap only behave if elements/keys implement equals() AND hashCode() consistently. A custom key class missing hashCode → contains says false for an equal object — the bug every Java interview asks about. Override equals() and hashCode() together, always.

"}, "D387/cheat/c4": {"body": "

📋 Concurrency

Condensed from your lessons — the rules, traps and topics of this chapter in one place.

Threads and Runnable

Core concepts — 1. What a thread is. An independent path of execution within a process. Each thread has its own stack but shares the heap with other threads in the same process. The OS…

Quick recap — A thread is an independent execution path. Define work with Runnable; create with new Thread(runnable); start with start() (never run()). Threads move through NEW →…

Glossary

Synchronization and Locks

⚠ SYNCHRONIZE THE SMALLEST THING THAT WORKS Locks serialize — too much synchronized and threads queue up (or deadlock if two locks are taken in opposite orders). Guard the shared mutable state, not entire workflows;…

Executor Framework

⚠ Runnable vs Callable, shutdown vs shutdownNow Runnable returns nothing; Callable returns a value (and can throw). shutdown() drains gracefully; shutdownNow() interrupts. Forgetting shutdown entirely leaves non-daemon…

CompletableFuture and Async

⚠ MATCH THE STAGE TO THE SHAPE Same shapes as functional interfaces: thenApply takes a Function (value→value), thenAccept a Consumer (value→void), thenRun a Runnable (ignores the value). Picking the wrong stage type is…

Concurrent Collections

⚠ KNOW THE ROSTER ConcurrentHashMap (shared maps), CopyOnWriteArrayList (read-heavy lists — every write copies the array), BlockingQueue (producer-consumer: put blocks when full, take blocks when empty). Match the collection to the access pattern and the concurrency question answers itself.

"}, "D387/cheat/c5": {"body": "

📋 Modern Java Features

Condensed from your lessons — the rules, traps and topics of this chapter in one place.

Optional

⚠ .get() DEFEATS THE PURPOSE Calling get() without checking is just a NullPointerException with a new name (NoSuchElementException). If you reach for get(), you wanted orElseThrow with a meaningful exception instead.

Records and Sealed Types

⚠ RECORDS CAN T EXTEND, CAN T MUTATE Records implicitly extend Record (no other superclass) and their components are final. Need mutable state or an inheritance hierarchy? A record is the wrong tool — that judgment…

Java Modules

⚠ PUBLIC IS NO LONGER ENOUGH Inside the module system, a public class in a NON-exported package cannot be touched from outside. public + exported is the new visibility rule — the single most-tested module fact.

Pattern Matching

⚠ ARROW CASES DON T FALL THROUGH switch expressions with -> have no fall-through and must be exhaustive (via sealed coverage or default). The old colon-switch rules don t apply — questions love mixing the two syntaxes.

"}, "D387/cheat/c6": {"body": "

📋 Design Patterns

Condensed from your lessons — the rules, traps and topics of this chapter in one place.

Creational Patterns

⚠ RECOGNIZE BY SYMPTOM Exactly one instance → Singleton. Telescoping constructors / many optional parameters → Builder. Creation logic varies by type, callers shouldn t know the class → Factory. Exams describe the…

Structural Patterns

⚠ ADAPTER CHANGES THE INTERFACE, DECORATOR KEEPS IT That one sentence separates them on every quiz. Wrapping + same interface + added behavior = decorator; wrapping + translated interface = adapter.

Behavioral Patterns

⚠ SPOT THEM IN THE WILD When X changes, notify all Y → Observer. Choose the algorithm at runtime → Strategy. Queue/undo user actions → Command. The behavioral patterns are recognized by their VERBS.

"}, "D387/cheat/c7": {"body": "

📋 Internationalization and I/O

Condensed from your lessons — the rules, traps and topics of this chapter in one place.

Internationalization and Locale

⚠ FILE NAMING IS THE MECHANISM messages_fr.properties matches Locale fr by NAME. Typo the suffix and you silently get English (fallback), not an error — the sneaky localization bug the PA makes you chase.

NIO.2 and the Path API

⚠ Path REPLACES File The legacy java.io.File returns booleans on failure (silently); NIO.2 throws IOException with real diagnostics, handles links/permissions, and streams directories. Which API should new code use? →…

Serialization and JSON

⚠ JSON vs JAVA SERIALIZATION Java s built-in Serializable produces a binary, Java-only format with known security issues; JSON is text, language-neutral, and web-standard. For APIs the answer is always JSON — typically via Jackson, the library the exam expects you to name for Java JSON handling.
